hook: Every system in this course leans on one truth: **the fastest query is the one you never run**. Redis makes state fast; document databases make state flexible. The last two tools in the belt.

scenes.title: Redis: a data structure server living in RAM
scenes.sub: Strings, hashes, sets, sorted sets — with TTLs on everything

do: update one field, not the blob

scenes.narration: Redis is best understood not as a database but as a REMOTE DATA-STRUCTURE SERVER: everything lives in memory, everything is one of a handful of structures, and every key can carry a TTL. The four structures cover most of systems programming: STRINGS for caching — get/set with EX seconds — the canonical pattern: check Redis, return on hit, compute on miss, store with a TTL; HASHES for objects — HSET session:user:42 field value — update one field without rewriting the blob; SETS for membership and dedupe — SADD seen:event:123 returns 0 if it was already there — this ONE command is your webhook idempotency (PY-14) and job-dedupe (AG-19) in a single round trip; and SORTED SETS for leaderboards, rate limits, and priority queues — ZADD + ZRANGEBYSCORE is a sliding-window rate limiter in three commands. Two properties shape everything: SPEED — sub-millisecond reads — Redis is where 'fast enough' actually lives; and VOLATILITY — memory is not disk — treat Redis as an accelerator and a scratchpad, never as the only copy of anything that matters.

scenes.title: Cache-aside, the pattern everything else builds on
scenes.body:
import redis.asyncio as redis

r = redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379")

async def get_report(user_id: int) -> Report:
    key = f"report:{user_id}"

    # 1 · look in the fast place first
    cached = await r.get(key)
    if cached:
        return Report.parse(cached)      # hit: ~0.5ms, done

    # 2 · miss: do the real work (DB query, LLM call, anything)
    report = await build_report(user_id)

    # 3 · store with a TTL — always a TTL:
    #    caches without expiry become distributed lies
    await r.set(key, report.to_json(), ex=300)   # 5 minutes
    return report

# Hit-rate math that justifies the pattern:
#   build_report cost: 400ms + LLM tokens
#   Redis hit:         0.5ms, zero tokens
#   hit-rate 95% → avg latency ~20ms, cost cut ~20x
annot: Cache-aside: check → compute → store — the app controls the cache, the database stays ignorant
ex=300 always — stale-forever caches serve yesterday's truth with today's confidence
The SADD/ZADD variants of this pattern power dedupe and rate limiting identically (PY-14's webhook replay guard)

scenes.title: Redis as infrastructure: locks, queues, pub/sub, and circuit breakers
scenes.sub: The Swiss army knife behind AG-19, PY-14, and AG-23

steps.at: Revisit the course through Redis-colored glasses

do: NX atomic · EX frees dead locks

scenes.narration: Revisit the course through Redis-colored glasses and it appears everywhere. QUEUES: LPUSH + BRPOP is a battle-tested work queue — AG-19's job queues can start here before graduating to a broker; the pattern — enqueue fast, workers pop blocking — needs no extra service. DEDUPE and IDEMPOTENCY: SADD with the job ID as member — atomic, single round trip — the webhook idempotency from PY-14 and exactly-once-ish processing from AG-19 share this one command. PUB/SUB: publish event, N subscribers react — the horizontal-scale backbone for WebSockets from PY-14 (replica A publishes, replica B forwards to its sockets); a caveat — pub/sub is FIRE-AND-FORGET — a subscriber that's down misses the message — so it carries signals, not state. RATE LIMITING: ZADD/ZREMRANGEBYSCORE/ZCARD implements a sliding window — the per-tenant circuit breaker AG-25 and AG-23 demand. And LOCKS: SET key NX EX is a distributed lock — the NX (not-exists) makes acquisition atomic, the EX prevents dead locks when a holder crashes — use for 'only one worker rebuilds the cache' — but keep the critical section tiny and never hold a lock across a network call you don't control.

scenes.title: Sliding-window rate limit + distributed lock
scenes.body:
# 1 · Sliding-window rate limit — AG-25's per-tenant breaker
async def allow(tenant: str, limit: int = 500) -> bool:
    key = f"rl:{tenant}"
    now = time.time()
    async with r.pipeline() as p:              # atomic batch
        p.zremrangebyscore(key, 0, now - 600)  # drop window ‐ 10min
        p.zadd(key, {f"{now}-{uuid4()}": now})
        p.zcard(key)
        p.expire(key, 600)
        _, _, count, _ = await p.execute()
    return count <= limit

# 2 · Distributed lock — one worker rebuilds the cache
async def with_lock(name: str, ttl: int = 30):
    token = uuid4().hex
    got = await r.set(f"lock:{name}", token, nx=True, ex=ttl)
    if not got:
        return                                # someone else is rebuilding
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        # release only if it's still OURS (token check —
        # the lock may have expired and been re-acquired)
        if await r.get(f"lock:{name}") == token:
            await r.delete(f"lock:{name}")
annot: pipeline() batches the four commands into one atomic round trip — no race between count and expiry
The token check on release is the subtle correctness bit — naive delete can free someone else's lock
limit per TENANT, window sliding — AG-25's noisy-neighbor defense, expressed in 10 lines

scenes.title: Cosmos DB and MongoDB: documents where the shape is the schema
scenes.sub: JSON in, JSON out — schema flexibility with real query power

do: match on nested fields · sharding built in

steps.at: anywhere the shape varies per record

scenes.narration: Document databases store JSON-like documents in collections — no migrations for shape changes, nested structures kept whole — the fit for the schema-thrash era of rapid product iteration and for the agent world, where a memory record (AG-17) or an agent definition (AG-25) IS a JSON document with evolving fields. MONGODB is the category's open-source standard: rich query language — match on nested fields, arrays, aggregation pipelines — horizontal sharding built in; COSMOS DB is Azure's globally-distributed managed document store: MongoDB API compatibility as one of several APIs, turnkey multi-region replication with conflict resolution — the managed choice when GA-29's Azure stack is already the platform. The query model, once: find filters by fields; aggregation pipelines transform — match, group, project, the same vocabulary as Polars (PY-16) wearing JSON; and indexes still matter — 'flexible schema' is not 'no indexes' — index what you filter on or every query is a collection scan. Where they fit in YOUR stack: user profiles, session state that outlives a TTL, event history, agent memory stores, content catalogs — anywhere the shape varies per record and joins are rare.

scenes.title: MongoDB: the 20% that covers 80%
scenes.body:
from motor.motor_asyncio import AsyncIOMotorClient

client = AsyncIOMotorClient("mongodb://localhost:27017")
db = client["lkg"]
mem = db["agent_memory"]          # AG-17's store, document edition

# 1 · write: a memory record IS the JSON you already have
await mem.update_one(
    {"user_id": uid, "kind": "preference"},
    {"$set": {"voice": "nova", "updated": now}},
    upsert=True,                   # create if missing — no migrations
)

# 2 · read with nested filters
async for doc in mem.find({"user_id": uid,
                           "updated": {"$gte": cutoff}}):
    ...

# 3 · aggregation pipeline — Polars vocabulary in JSON
pipeline = [
    {"$match": {"kind": "session"}},
    {"$group": {"_id": "$user_id", "n": {"$sum": 1}}},
    {"$sort": {"n": -1}}, {"$limit": 10},
]
top_users = await mem.aggregate(pipeline).to_list(length=None)
annot: upsert=True — the write-once shape of agent memory; new fields appear without a migration
Nested filters read like the document shape — dot paths match the JSON you stored
match/group/sort/limit — if you just learned Polars expressions (PY-16), aggregation pipelines are the same brain

scenes.title: Choosing your store: the decision that quietly decides your architecture
scenes.sub: Postgres, Redis, documents — a one-paragraph policy

steps.at: The course has now handed you
DOCUMENT DB is the escape hatch
pick the one your team can operate

scenes.narration: The course has now handed you four storage tools — Postgres (GA-10's relational + vector workhorse), Redis, and document databases — and the final architectural skill is a DEFAULT POLICY you can state in one breath. RELATIONAL (Postgres) is the system of record: structured data, transactions, relations, vectors via pgvector — start EVERY project here until a need proves otherwise — the moment you have two stores, consistency questions multiply; REDIS is the accelerator on top: cache, locks, rate limits, pub/sub, lightweight queues — anything rebuildable, anything needing sub-millisecond speed — never the system of record; DOCUMENT DB is the escape hatch for genuinely shape-varying data at scale — profiles, catalogs, event streams — or when global distribution is the requirement (Cosmos). The failure mode to avoid is store sprawl — each new database is a new operational lifeform: backups, versions, dashboards, on-call knowledge — AG-25's platform discipline applies to storage too. When torn between two options: pick the one your team can operate in their sleep, and let the exotic one earn its place with a measured benchmark. That's the whole craft — and with that, the toolkit is complete.

scenes.title: The storage policy, as a comment block
scenes.body:
# STORAGE POLICY (one breath, memorized):
#
#   Postgres   → system of record. Everything starts here.
#                Relations, transactions, pgvector — GA-10.
#   Redis      → accelerator. Cache, locks, limits, pub/sub,
#                queues — anything rebuildable, sub-ms (this reel).
#   Documents  → escape hatch. Shape-varying data at scale,
#                global distribution — Cosmos/MongoDB.
#
# Anti-pattern: store sprawl — every new DB is a new lifeform
# to feed (backups, dashboards, on-call). AG-25's platform
# discipline applies to storage FIRST.
#
# Tie-breaker: choose what your team operates in their sleep;
# make the exotic option EARN its place with a benchmark.
annot: 'Everything starts in Postgres' — the sentence that prevents most over-engineering
Rebuildable data only in Redis — volatility is a feature for caches, a bug for ledgers
Benchmarks arbitrate — GA-20's eval discipline applied to infrastructure choices

EIGHTY REELS, one idea repeated until it's instinct: MODELS ARE PROBABILISTIC, so systems earn trust through EVALS (GA-20), guardrails (AG-09), budgets (AG-23), and honest gates (GA-30). The course arc mirrors a real engagement: learn the tools, build pipelines, ship to production, then architect for others. recap: Redis is a remote data-structure server: strings for cache (always with TTL), sets for dedupe, sorted sets for rate limits — sub-millisecond, volatile by design
Cache-aside (check → compute → store) plus pipelines, locks with token-checked release, and sliding-window limiters cover Redis's 80%
Document databases (MongoDB / Cosmos DB) keep JSON whole — flexible schema, aggregation pipelines share Polars' vocabulary, indexes still mandatory
Storage policy in one breath: Postgres is the record, Redis the accelerator, documents the escape hatch — store sprawl is the enemy

quiz.q: Why does every cached value need a TTL — what failure does it prevent?
opts: Redis runs out of memory immediately without one
A cache entry without expiry can serve stale data forever — quietly turning your fast path into a source of yesterday's truth; TTL bounds staleness by construction
It's required for the SET command to work
quiz.why: Unexpired caches are distributed lies: upstream data changes, the cache keeps serving the old value with full confidence. A TTL makes staleness a bounded, designed property instead of an accident.

quiz.q: What makes SET key value NX EX the correct primitive for a distributed lock?
opts: NX makes acquisition atomic (only one client wins) and EX bounds the hold — a crashed holder's lock self-releases instead of deadlocking everyone
EX forces other clients to wait politely
It's the only command Redis supports for locking
quiz.why: Two correctness properties in one command: atomic acquire (NX = set only if not exists) and automatic expiry (EX) so a dead worker can't hold the lock forever. The token check on release closes the last gap (expired-and-reacquired).

quiz.q: Your team debates adding MongoDB for a new feature. What's the policy from this reel?
opts: Always add it — document databases are modern
Start in Postgres as the system of record; only adopt a document DB when data shape genuinely varies per record or global distribution is the requirement — and make it earn its place with a benchmark
Add it if the developers prefer its syntax
quiz.why: Store sprawl is real operational cost. The policy: Postgres until proven otherwise, Redis for rebuildable speed, documents for shape-varying/global data — and the exotic option earns its slot with measurements, not preference.

code.title: The last snippet of the course
code.body:
# Reel 80 of 80 — the pattern that ties the course together:
# every fast system in these reels has the same skeleton.

async def serve(request):
    await guardrails.check(request)              # AG-09
    if not await rate_limit.allow(request.tenant):   # this reel
        return slow_down()

    cached = await redis.get(key(request))       # this reel
    if cached:
        return cached

    async with lock("rebuild"):                  # this reel
        result = await agent.answer(             # AG-14
            request.text,
            memory=await mongo.load(request.user),   # AG-17
            eval_log=True,                       # AG-21
        )
    await redis.set(key(request), result, ex=300)
    return result
# COURSE COMPLETE. Now go build the one only you can build.

notes:
# NoSQL & Cache — PY notes

## Redis
- Data-structure server in RAM: strings, hashes, sets, sorted sets.
- Cache-aside: get → compute → set EX. TTLs always.
- SADD = idempotency/dedupe (PY-14, AG-19). ZADD pipeline = sliding-window rate limit (AG-25, AG-23).
- SET NX EX = distributed lock; release with token check.
- Pub/sub = WebSocket fanout backbone (PY-14); fire-and-forget — signals, not state.
- Never the system of record.

## Document DBs (MongoDB / Cosmos DB)
- JSON whole; flexible schema; upsert without migrations.
- Aggregation pipelines = match/group/sort — Polars vocabulary (PY-16) in JSON.
- Index what you filter on — flexible schema ≠ no indexes.
- Cosmos: MongoDB API + turnkey multi-region on the GA-29 stack.

## Storage policy
Postgres = record (start here) · Redis = accelerator · Documents = escape hatch. Store sprawl is the enemy; exotic options earn their slot via benchmark (GA-20 discipline).

## Course close
80 reels: PY (01-25), GA (01-30), AG (01-25). Core idea: probabilistic models → trust through evals, guardrails, budgets, gates. Keep the reels as a cross-linked reference; practice by rebuilding without looking.
